newsitem.title: USA: Republicans hope for Georgia congressional victory.
newsitem.headline: Republicans hope for Georgia congressional victory.

text.p: If there is one Democratic incumbent that Republicans hope to unseat in this year's congressional campaign in the South, political analysts say it is U.S. Representative Cynthia McKinney of Georgia.

The 41-year-old, unabashed liberal, who lost her former black-majority district in a Supreme Court ruling to redraw the district last year, finds her campaign against a Jewish Republican embroiled in charges of anti-Semitism with less than three weeks to go before the November election.

"It's probably alienated her largest group of liberal white voters, and that would be the Jewish community. And she was already on awfully thin ice with them," said Charles Bullock, a political science professor at the University of Georgia.

McKinney, the first black woman to be elected to Congress from Georgia, is running in the state's newly drawn 4th District, which encompasses the Dekalb County neighbourhoods east of Atlanta as well as a portion of the city's mainly conservative northern suburbs.
The district is home to Georgia's largest Jewish community, which makes up about 10 percent of the white vote and traditionally ranks as a bastion of support for Democratic candidates.
McKinney needs the backing of about one-third of white voters along with solid support from the area's 35-percent black electorate if she is to carry the district.

Her opponent, political novice John Mitnick, has been trying to sway Jews and other white voters against McKinney by underscoring her refusal to support a congressional resolution decrying the hate speech of an aide to Nation of Islam Minister Louis Farrakhan.

The controversy boiled over this week, when McKinney's father resigned from her campaign after branding Mitnick "a racist Jew" during remarks at the Ebenezer Baptist Church in Atlanta, the sanctuary where slain civil rights leader Martin Luther King once preached.
Democratic Party officials believe McKinney can weather the storm, pointing to large contingents of liberal white voters who inhabit the residential neighbourhoods near Atlanta's Emory University.
But analysts say the damage wrought by the remarks of her father, Billy McKinney, a former Atlanta policeman and civil rights activist, may be irreparable this late in the campaign.

"A few weeks ago, I still would have bet on her to win. Now I think I wouldn't. I think she is going to run way behind the normal Democratic vote in those areas," said Alan Abramowitz, a political scientist at Emory University.
Neither McKinney nor Mitnick returned repeated telephone calls.
McKinney's seat could prove crucial to a Republican struggle against Democrats for control of the House of Representatives.

The party of Lincoln holds a 235 to 198 advantage in the chamber. But Republicans are expected to pick up only a handful of House seats in the South, a region they hoped would insulate them from potentially large losses in other parts of the country. Democrats need to add about 20 seats to gain House control.

Mitnick, a 34-year-old self-proclaimed moderate who favours abortion and some gun control, could appeal to left-of-centre voters despite his penchant for conservative fiscal policies, which include an overhauled tax system.

But McKinney already has badly embarrassed political experts by winning the Democratic primary with enough votes to avoid a runoff. In that victory, she polled about 25 percent of the white electorate.
Much now depends on how non-Jewish white voters perceive her candidacy.

"She ran an unnecessarily negative campaign against the other candidates in the primary and, although she won very easily, I think she antagonized some liberals and moderates whose votes she's going to need," said Abramowitz.
